title: Two pointers
summary: Move two indices in one pass when each move throws away a region.

parts.rule: Move two indices through a sequence so each step permanently discards a region. The whole scan stays linear when every index only advances.
parts.why: Pair sums on a sorted array, in-place partitioning, and palindrome checks often waste a nested search. Two pointers replace that nest with one coordinated pass.
parts.example: SAMPLE: a sorted array and a target sum. Place one index at the start and one at the end. If the sum is too small, advance the left. If too large, pull the right backward. Each move throws away impossible pairs without restarting.

body:
Rule. Move two indices through a sequence so each step permanently discards a region. The whole scan stays linear when every index only advances.

Why it matters. Pair sums on a sorted array, in-place partitioning, and palindrome checks often waste a nested search. Two pointers replace that nest with one coordinated pass.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: a sorted array and a target sum. Place one index at the start and one at the end. If the sum is too small, advance the left. If too large, pull the right backward. Each move throws away impossible pairs without restarting.

When to use. Apply two pointers on sorted inputs, on opposite-end comparisons, and on slow/fast pointer cycles in lists. Combine with a write index when compacting in place.

When to refuse. Refuse the pattern on unsorted data when order is required for correctness unless you sort first and accept that cost. Refuse moving a pointer backward and forward in ways that re-examine the same indices enough to lose the linear bound.
